documentation.range:
This species is endemic to Madagascar and is currently only known from the Moramanga District, in the central-east of the island. 

The 2008 IUCN Red List assessment described the range as being "centered on the Torotofotsy area (c. 7 km northeast of Andasibe) and the Andromena Forest at the Samarirana River [...] with several other small forest fragments north and south of Moramanga" (Vences and Raxworthy 2008). 

Bora et al. (2008) confirmed the presence of the species at 16 localities. Randrianavelona et al. (2010) surveyed those 16 localities and an additional 17, where various sources had reported the occurrence of the species, and confirmed that it was extant at 26 of the 33 known localities. The seven localities where the species was not detected have been converted or degraded between 2003–2008 (Randrianavelona et al. 2010). Between 2010–2013, Piludu et al. (2015) visited 23 of the 26 localities confirmed by Randrianavelona et al. (2010) and an additional 186 breeding ponds, and confirmed the species' presence in 139 ponds. However, the paper states that some ponds occur near each other and could count as a single locality, but it does not offer a revised number of localities. This should be clarified in the future. Two notable outliers at Analabe and the Ambakoana forest located to the north of Moramanga were verified in 2007 by Bora et al. (2008), but the forest at these sites is reported to have been destroyed, no surveys have been conducted there since 2008, and the species is feared to have disappeared from this part of its range (R.R. Andriantsimanarilafy pers. comm. March 2018). 

The results of these surveys show that extant localities can be grouped into two general areas: 1) Ambatovy-Torotofotsy (or Analamay) northeast of Moramanga, and 2) Andranomena-Mangabe forest southwest of Moramanga. All but one site is east of the Mangoro River. The current distribution map reflects this expansion and the grouping of confirmed, extant records into these two areas, which are separated by ca. 35 km (R.R. Andriantsimanarilafy pers. comm. 2018). The validity of record at the Sahasarotra forest locality of Bora et al. (2008) to the southeast of Moramanga is uncertain (R.R. Andriantsimanarilafy pers. comm. 2018).

The elevational range of this species has been updated from 920–960 m asl (Vences and Raxworthy 2008) to 867–1,065 m asl (Bora et al. 2008, Randrianavelona et al. 2010). Its extent of occurrence (EOO) was reported as 626 km2 in Andreone and Randriamahazo (2008) and was increased by Piludu et al. (2015) to 699 km2. The EOO of the 2008 distribution, as calculated by the IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group, was 539 km2 and the EOO of the 2018 distribution is 730 km2. This increase is due to the additional ponds identified by Piludu et al. (2015). The area of occupancy (AOO) of confirmed records in Piludu et al. (2015) is 152 km2. The distribution is thought to be divided into two threat-defined locations: 1) Ambatovy-Torotofotsy and 2) Andranomena-Mangabe.
documentation.population:
There are a few estimates available of the abundance or density of this species and these range from 500–3,000 individuals ha-1 (Behra et al. 1995) to 836–1,371 individuals ha-1 (Rabemananjara et al. 2008). There is no published information on temporal (seasonal and annual) or spatial (inter-site) variation in the local population abundance.

The findings of Piludu et al. (2015) do not represent an increase in population size. Instead, the increased number of known breeding sites was associated with an increase in survey effort. However, Piludu et al. (2015) reported that 50% of the 139 confirmed ponds were actively affected by habitat loss, that seven had been lost since 2008 due to agricultural expansion and illegal gold mining, and an additional eight ponds were projected to be lost due to legal nickel and cobalt mining "in the near future". In addition, Randrianavelona et al. (2010) reported the loss of seven sites between 2003–2008 due to habitat destruction and conversion to agriculture. The species was also confirmed as occurring at the two northernmost known sites at Analabe and the Ambakoana forest in 2007, but these have since been lost.

Based on the ongoing decline in quality and extent of suitable habitat, and the ongoing harvesting of individuals from the wild for the pet trade, the population is inferred to be decreasing at an unknown rate. It is also thought that the population is severely fragmented.
documentation.habitats: This species inhabits mid-elevation humid forests and its often associated with Pandanus swamp (Vences et al. 1999, Andreone et al. 2005). Adult frogs are found under leaf litter, dead logs, and in tree-root cavities in the forest surrounding breeding pools during the austral winter. The species requires small lentic wetlands for reproduction and adults aggregate around them during the breeding season (Randrianavelona et al. 2010 - Stratégie de Conservation). The eggs are laid on the ground, and the larvae are flushed by rain into swamps, temporary ponds, and flooded forest, where they develop further. It appears to tolerate a degree of moderate forest disturbance and occupies a range of sites that vary both in vegetation structure and fragment size (Andreone et al. 2005). Adults have been observed in recently burned forest, but the viability of these post-fire breeding sites is uncertain (Andreone et al. 2005).
documentation.threats:
The species is currently restricted to fragments of forest surrounded by degraded land. The remaining forest is under threat from subsistence agriculture, timber extraction, legal and illegal natural resource extraction, fires, and expanding human settlements.

Expanding small-scale agriculture and both artisanal and industrial mining are the primary threats to this species because they can result in rapid and complete destruction of breeding ponds over a wide area (Piludu et al. 2015). Surveys reported in the 2008 assessment, indicated that the habitat was being degraded in all areas where the species was known to occur, and that in 2001 a significant amount of the remaining suitable habitat at Torotorofotsy was affected by fire (although three years later the species was still common in the affected areas). Piludu et al. (2015) estimated that 50% of the 139 ponds with confirmed sightings were actively threatened with habitat destruction, even though 51% of the ponds are located inside provisional protected areas. 

A current concern is the spread of the invasive Asian Common toad (Duttaphrynus melanostictus), which was first recorded in Madagascar in Toamasina in March 2014 (Kolby 2014). A species distribution model by Pearson (2015) suggests that there is a high probability of this invasive toad occurring in the range of this species, increasing the risk of disease transmission and food-web disruption (Piludu et al. 2015).

It is possible that over-collecting for commercial and private purposes is a threat, but so far harvesting levels have not had a visible effect on its population. Species in this genus have also tested positive for Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), however currently there have been no negative effects observed within amphibian populations in Madagascar suggesting the Bd strain has a low virulence level (Bletz et al. 2015).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions In-Place
Piludu et al. (2015) reported 51% of known sites as occurring within protected areas. Conservation activities to protect habitat are underway at the Torotorofotsy Ramsar site. Similarly, the forest at Mangabe, southwest of Moramanga, was established as a protected area in 2015 as a sustainable use protected area. However, both these sites currently lack strong enforcement and reductions in habitat quality and extent are ongoing. The sites that occur within the perimeters of the Ambatovy mine, northeast of Moramanga, currently receive effective protection, but the long-term future of these sites is uncertain and some are expected to be lost. 

A species conservation strategy was launched in February 2011 by the government of Madagascar that set out the key steps over the next five years to maintain this species in the wild (Randrianavelona et al. 2010 - Stratégie de Conservation). This species has also been assessed through Amphibian Ark as being in need of ex-situ conservation efforts (D. Edmonds pers. comm. November 2015) and many zoos and aquaria have responded to this need. There is also a genetically viable assurance colony being maintained in captivity near Andasibe, within the species' native range, by Association Mitsinjo (D. Edmonds pers. comm. November 2015, Edmonds et al. 2015).

Conservation Actions Needed
In general, improved management and protection of the breeding ponds--both inside and outside protected areas--is required. In particular, the identification of sites at which collection is taking place is required, followed by careful management of these sites and long-term monitoring of the population in order to assess the impact of this activity on the species (R.R. Andriantsimanarilafy pers. comm. August 2018). 

Research Needed
There is a need to learn more about the natural history and population parameters of this species in order to support evidence-based conservation interventions (Piludu et al. 2015). Surveys in some areas may also be warranted to confirm the anecdotal reports of the species' presence. Research is essential to fully understand the distribution, origin, type and virulence of Bd lineages found in Madagascar (Bletz et al. 2015).
documentation.use_trade:
This species has been collected from the wild for use in national and international trade, as well as scientific research. It is popular in the exotic pet trade (Rabemananjara et al. 2008) and uses of this species include commercial display in zoos and aquaria, as well as, in private collections. It is held in a number of private and public institutions, mainly in North America and Europe. A total captive population of 694 frogs was reported from 51 different institutions for 2009 (www.species360.org).

There is little information on the domestic use of this species, but live individuals are known to be housed in the Croc Farm (Antananarivo), Parc Botanique and Zoologique de Tsimbazaza (Antananarivo), and the Madagascar Exotic Park (Mandraka). This species is also used to promote tourism and conservation in Madagascar (www.parcs-madagascar.com). It is also the emblem of the Torotorofotsy RAMSAR site near Andasibe.

Since 1995, the trade in wild individuals of this species has been monitored by CITES. The species accounted for 50% of the Mantella frogs imported from Madagascar between 1994 and 2003 (Rabemananjara et al. 2008), with North America (United States and Canada) and western Europe being the largest importers of Mantella frogs (Rabemananjara et al. 2008). A quota of 2,500 frogs was agreed by CITES in 2009. The consequences of increasing the quota from zero to 2,500 individuals in 2009 is unknown. Currently, CITES-recorded exports of this species seem to be on the order of a few hundred each year (CITES 2018).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Endangered because its extent of occurrence (EOO) is between 699-730 km<sup>2</sup>, there is ongoing decline in its area of occupancy (AOO) of 152 km<sup>2</sup>, it occurs in two threat-defined locations, its population is severely fragmented, the extent of its forest habitat in east-central Madagascar is declining, and the number of mature individuals might also be declining through over-exploitation.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: There are populations of "golden" mantellas that might belong to other species. The taxonomy of this group is uncertain but the definition of Mantella aurantiaca is clear and there seems to be little genetic subdivision within the species (M. Vences pers. comm.).
